nameStory: The "Clingy Square Britches" name comes from this lichen's habit of forming neat, squarish lobes that hug tightly to tree bark like well-fitted pants. The "clingy" part refers to how firmly it attaches to its host, often requiring careful prying to remove intact specimens.
description: Clingy Square Britches is a medium-sized foliose (leaf-like) lichen that forms neat patches of gray-green lobes on tree bark. Each colony typically spans 2-4 inches across, made up of overlapping, roughly square-shaped sections that lie flat against the bark. The surface has a subtle powdery appearance, especially around the edges, and the whole lichen feels papery-thin but surprisingly tough when dry.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leaf-like patches with distinctly square to rectangular lobes that overlap like roof shingles, lying very close to the bark surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale gray-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; the underside is black with scattered pale spots

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly wrinkled surface with a faint powdery coating, especially noticeable along lobe edges; feels like thin parchment when touched

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring oak, maple, and ash trees in somewhat protected locations

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Rarely produces the cup-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia); instead reproduces mainly through tiny powdery granules (soredia) along lobe margins

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are typically 0.2-0.4 inches wide, with entire colonies reaching 2-4 inches across when mature

habitat: Clingy Square Britches grows on the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests and older woodlands throughout New England's lower elevations. It prefers somewhat sheltered locations with moderate humidity, often found on the north-facing sides of oak, maple, and ash trees. Look for it in established forests rather than young woods or forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring rains wet the surface, making identification easier. This is an excellent time to observe the color change from dry gray to moist green.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat bleached or pale gray during dry periods, but the square lobe pattern remains clearly visible. Summer humidity can bring out subtle color variations.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as deciduous trees lose their leaves, providing clearer views of bark-dwelling specimens. Colors may be particularly rich during moist fall weather.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round and may actually stand out more against snow-covered bark. Winter moisture from snow and ice can intensify the green coloration.

funFact: Despite being incredibly thin - thinner than a sheet of paper - Clingy Square Britches can live for decades and will actually outlive many of the trees it grows on, sometimes transferring to nearby bark when its original host falls!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other gray-green foliose lichens, but the distinctly square lobe shape is diagnostic. Remember: "Square britches, square lobes" - if the lobes are rounded or irregular, you're looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: This lichen is quite rare in New England with only 5 recorded observations, making any sighting noteworthy for citizen science projects. It's more common in southeastern United States, so New England represents the northern edge of its range.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Powder-tipped Antler Lichen which has more irregular, branching lobes, Clingy Square Britches maintains those characteristic square-shaped segments. The Powdered Loop Lichen has distinctly rolled lobe edges and a whiter underside, while Showman's Loop Lichen tends to form larger, more circular patches with less geometric lobe shapes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its loop lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Antler Lichen has the narrowest, most antler-like lobes and the most abundant powdery soredia.
